content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has identified multimodal improvement strategies (MMIS) as the most effective approach for implementing infection prevention and control (IPC) interventions. This conclusion is based on the development of the WHO hand hygiene MMIS, which has demonstrated significant effectiveness in various studies. The concept of MMIS has since been expanded to include any intervention aimed at improving IPC practices, as outlined in the WHO guidelines on core components for IPC programs. MMIS is designated as Core Component 5 in these guidelines, which are supported by the highest volume of evidence among all components. WHO recommends that IPC activities at both national and facility levels should be implemented using MMIS. At the national level, this involves coordination by the national IPC team. In primary care facilities, MMIS should focus on improving hand hygiene, safe injection practices, decontamination of medical instruments, and environmental cleaning. In secondary care facilities, MMIS should address standard and transmission-based precautions and triage. In tertiary care facilities, MMIS should target standard and transmission-based precautions, triage, and the reduction of specific infections in high-risk areas or patient groups, aligned with local priorities. The implementation of IPC interventions should follow a stepwise approach, beginning with a thorough assessment of the current IPC practices and local activities. WHO proposes a five-step implementation cycle, grounded in implementation and quality improvement science, to guide the planning and management of IPC interventions. This cycle should be continuously applied and updated over several years to maximize impact and sustainability. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) advises that the MMIS approach and the five-step cycle can also be applied to the implementation of other IPC guidelines. Countries and healthcare facilities should evaluate their local guidelines and standard operating procedures for preventing bloodstream infections (BSIs) and other infections associated with peripheral catheters. This evaluation should determine whether updates are needed to align with WHO guidelines. Local practices should also be assessed to identify common gaps, enabling the development of targeted improvement plans based on relevant recommendations and good practice statements. Peripheral intravenous catheters (PIVCs) are among the most commonly used devices in healthcare worldwide, but their safe use requires further research. Issues such as insertion techniques, maintenance, and removal need to be clarified to improve safety and practicality. For example, research is needed to optimize sterile and aseptic no-touch insertion techniques, the use of chlorhexidine-containing skin disinfectants, and the effectiveness of formal training on catheter insertion. Additionally, the development of cost-effective materials for single-use gloves and standardized insertion kits could enhance accessibility, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). The use of ultrasound-guided assistance for catheter insertion, the selection of optimal insertion sites, and the comparison of upper versus lower limb insertion also require further investigation. Research into the benefits of occlusive catheter dressings, the use of local anesthetics during insertion, and the impact of catheter management practices, such as regular tubing changes and the use of saline versus anticoagulant solutions, is also necessary. Catheter removal protocols, including scheduled versus clinically indicated removal and the timing of removal for catheters inserted under emergency conditions, need to be better defined. Studies should explore the risks associated with prolonged catheter placement and the potential benefits of using formal insertion teams. Finally, research is needed to determine the clinical scenarios in which single-lumen versus multi-lumen peripherally inserted central catheters (PICCs) are required, as well as the advantages of PICCs compared to midline catheters (MCVs) or PIVCs. This research will help develop universal protocols for catheter selection and management, ensuring safer and more effective use of these devices in diverse healthcare settings.
